22.title: Before anything, a voice (Genesis 1:1–5)
22.hook: the Torah opens "in the beginning" and speaks light into the dark
22.howItsDone: Jews read Bereshit as the first weekly Torah portion each autumn, right after Simchat Torah, and the first chapter of Genesis is studied closely in Jewish learning.

segments.voice: Yesterday: the parsha, the weekly portion, and camp one's twenty-one words. Your line was join the cycle wherever it is. Now camp two: the stories, the original serial, told one episode at a time by a whole people for generations.
screen: `THE PARSHA — JOIN THE CYCLE.` → `CAMP TWO: THE STORIES.`

segments.voice: No light. No ground. No sky. The text calls it unformed and void: darkness over the deep, and a wind, or a spirit, hovering over the water. Nothing has happened yet, and nobody is there to see it. Then, before any thing, before a single star, there's a sound. Someone speaks.
screen: `DARKNESS OVER THE DEEP.` → `NOBODY THERE TO SEE IT.` → `THEN, A VOICE.`

segments.voice: The Torah's first word is Bereshit: in the beginning. It also names the whole book of Genesis, and the first weekly portion. In the Jewish Publication Society's 1917 translation: "In the beginning God created the heaven and the earth." Even that first word is argued over. The medieval commentator Rashi pointed out that the grammar reads more like "in the beginning of God's creating," setting a scene rather than announcing the very first moment. Scholars still debate it. The rabbis also noticed the first letter, bet. It's closed on three sides and open only toward the front, the way Hebrew is read. One midrash calls that a hint: what came before, what's above and below, isn't yours to chase. Start here, and go forward. Then the first thing God does isn't build or shape. It's speak. "And God said: 'Let there be light.' And there was light." A sentence, and the world answers. The Mishnah says the world was created with ten sayings. And the day closes: "And there was evening and there was morning, one day." Not the first day. One day, with nothing yet to count against. So the Torah opens with the idea that words make things. The book of Proverbs says it plainly: "Death and life are in the power of the tongue."
screen: `BERESHIT — IN THE BEGINNING.` · `BET: CLOSED BEHIND, OPEN AHEAD.` · `LET THERE BE LIGHT.` · `TEN SAYINGS MADE THE WORLD.` · then, large: `DEATH AND LIFE ARE IN THE POWER OF THE TONGUE.`

segments.voice: Close your eyes and let it be dark for a moment, the way the story starts. Think of someone you'll talk to today, and find one kind sentence that's true of them: specific, not a compliment you'd give anybody. When it's exactly right, say it once, softly, out loud.
Bereshit. In the beginning: the Torah's first word, where God speaks and light answers.
Your line: words make worlds. The Torah's first act is a sentence. That's day twenty-two.

23.title: Six days of making (Genesis 1:6–31)
23.hook: sky, sea, land, lights, creatures, each day closing "and it was good"
23.howItsDone: Jews read the six days of creation in the first Torah portion each autumn, and in the daily morning prayers praise God who renews the work of creation every day.

segments.voice: Yesterday: Bereshit, in the beginning. God spoke, and light answered. Your line was words make worlds.

An empty apartment fills up in a certain order. First the rooms: walls, a floor, a window that lets the light in. Then what fills them: a lamp in the corner, fish in a tank, a cat on the sill, people around a table. Nobody hangs a picture before there's a wall. The first chapter of Genesis is built a lot like that apartment.
screen: `AN EMPTY APARTMENT.` → `FIRST THE ROOMS.` → `THEN WHAT FILLS THEM.`

segments.voice: Here are the six days. One: light, separated from dark. Two: a dome of sky, between the waters above and the waters below. Three: dry land, and plants growing on it. Four: the sun, the moon and the stars. Five: fish in the sea and birds in the sky. Six: animals on the land, and then human beings. Some readers see a pattern. The first three days make spaces: day, sky and sea, land. The next three fill them, in the same order: lights, then fish and birds, then creatures of the land. Rooms, then furniture. Now a puzzle the rabbis loved: light on day one, but no sun until day four. So what was that first light? The Talmud says it was a special light, by which a person could see from one end of the world to the other, and God hid it away for the righteous in the time to come. The text never even names the sun and moon. It calls them the greater light and the lesser light, lamps set in the sky to do a job. And yom, the word for day? Jewish readers have disagreed about whether these are days of twenty-four hours; the chapter doesn't stop to say. What it does say, again and again, is that each thing is made "after its kind," fully itself. You met the refrain on day six: and it was good. Then, at the end of the sixth day, looking at everything together: "and, behold, it was very good."
screen: `THREE DAYS OF ROOMS.` · `THREE DAYS TO FILL THEM.` · `LIGHT BEFORE THE SUN.` · `EACH AFTER ITS KIND.` · then, large: `AND, BEHOLD, IT WAS VERY GOOD.`

segments.voice: Look around slowly and name six good things you can see, one for each day of making. Light, the sky or air through a window, something that grew, something that shines, something alive, and a person or a trace of one, like a photo or your own hands. Say each one quietly, then let the list sit.
Yom, the Hebrew word for day, and one the rabbis debated. Three days of rooms, three of filling them, and the good counted all the way through.
Your line: count the good. The chapter keeps that count right to the end. Day twenty-three, done.

24.title: In the image (Genesis 1:26–27)
24.hook: every person is made in God's image; the rabbis say a king's coins look alike, but God's people never do (Mishnah Sanhedrin 4:5)
24.howItsDone: Jewish teaching and law draw on tzelem Elohim for the dignity of every person, from the care of the sick to the honor given to the dead; the Mishnah's saying about saving one life as saving a whole world is widely quoted.

segments.voice: Yesterday: yom, the day. Three days of rooms, three days of filling them. Your line was count the good.

Take two coins of the same kind. Same face on both, a president or a queen, down to the last line of the hair. That's the point of a coin: stamped from one die, identical, interchangeable. Nobody cares which quarter they get. Now think of any ten people. Not one of them is the same. Nearly two thousand years ago, the rabbis put those two facts side by side, and made them one of the boldest teachings in Jewish law.
screen: `TWO COINS, THE SAME FACE.` → `TEN PEOPLE, NO TWO ALIKE.` → `THE RABBIS PUT THEM TOGETHER.`

segments.voice: On the sixth day, the Torah slows down. In the Jewish Publication Society's 1917 translation: "And God created man in His own image, in the image of God created He him; male and female created He them." In Hebrew: tzelem Elohim. Tzelem is an image, a likeness, the word for a statue or a figure. Elohim is God. Every human being carries God's likeness. What that likeness is, the Torah doesn't say. Maimonides said the mind, the ability to understand. Others say freedom, the power to choose, or to create, or to love. Now the coins. The Mishnah, describing how judges warned witnesses in a capital case, puts it this way. A human king stamps many coins with one seal, and they all look alike. The King of kings stamped every person with the seal of the first human, and not one is like another. God's image makes us different, not the same. Then it goes further. Why was humanity created from a single person? So that whoever destroys one life is as if they destroyed a whole world, and whoever saves one life, as if they saved a whole world. So no one can say to anyone else, my ancestor was greater than yours. And so each person is obliged to say: the world was created for my sake. Two rabbis once argued over the Torah's greatest principle. Rabbi Akiva said: love your neighbor as yourself. Ben Azzai pointed to the verse about humanity made in God's likeness, and said his was greater, because it covers everyone.
screen: `TZELEM ELOHIM — THE IMAGE OF GOD.` · `WHAT IS THE IMAGE? IT DOESN'T SAY.` · `ONE SEAL, NO TWO ALIKE.` · `ONE LIFE IS A WHOLE WORLD.` · then, large: `IN THE IMAGE OF GOD CREATED HE HIM.`

segments.voice: Picture a face you passed recently and barely noticed: a cashier, a driver, someone on the street. See it clearly, down to the one detail that's theirs and nobody else's. If you believe what the verse says, see God's image there; if you don't, see one entire world.
Tzelem Elohim. The image of God, stamped on every person, so that no two are alike.
Your line: no two faces alike. One seal, and every face its own. See you tomorrow.

25.title: The seventh day (Genesis 2:1–3)
25.hook: God finishes, then stops, and blesses the stopping itself
25.howItsDone: On Friday night, many Jews recite Genesis 2:1–3, beginning with the word vayechulu, at the start of kiddush over wine, closing the week with the story of the seventh day.

segments.voice: Yesterday: tzelem Elohim, the image of God, one seal and not one face like another. Your line was no two faces alike.

Friday night in a Jewish home. The candles are lit, the table is set. Someone stands and lifts a full cup of wine, and before any blessing over it, recites three verses from Genesis, the ones right after the six days of making. In homes that keep this custom, the week closes with those words every Friday night. They tell of the day God stopped.
screen: `FRIDAY NIGHT. A FULL CUP.` → `THREE VERSES FROM GENESIS.` → `THE DAY GOD STOPPED.`

segments.voice: The heaven and the earth are finished, the story says, and all their host. Then, in the Jewish Publication Society's 1917 translation: "And on the seventh day God finished His work which He had made." Wait. Finished on the seventh? Wasn't the work done on the sixth? The rabbis noticed. Rashi, quoting an older midrash, offers one answer: after six days the world had everything but one thing. Rest. Menuchah. So on the seventh day rest was created, and only then was the work complete. A world without stopping wasn't finished. Then: "And God blessed the seventh day, and hallowed it." Hallowed means made holy. In Hebrew it's the first time anything in the Torah is called holy, and it isn't a mountain, a temple or a person. It's a day. A stretch of time. The twentieth-century rabbi Abraham Joshua Heschel made that detail the heart of his book The Sabbath. One more thing. Every other day of creation closes with "there was evening and there was morning." The seventh doesn't. Some readers take that as a hint that the rest it started is still open. The text doesn't explain. So the story ends not with a final product but with a pause, and the pause is the part that's blessed. Finished isn't when the last thing is made. It's when you stop.
screen: `FINISHED ON THE SEVENTH DAY?` · `THE MISSING PIECE WAS REST.` · `THE FIRST HOLY THING IS A DAY.` · `NO EVENING, NO MORNING.` · then, large: `AND GOD BLESSED THE SEVENTH DAY.`

segments.voice: Today the practice is simply to stop: put down whatever is in your hands, and don't plan, tidy your thoughts or try to relax properly. If a task comes to mind, let it wait outside the door; nothing needs making for this minute to be complete. If you pray, the stopping itself can be the prayer.
Menuchah: the rest the seventh day needed to be finished. The day God stopped, blessed the stopping, and called a stretch of time holy.
Your line: finished is holy. The Sabbath you met on day eleven starts right here. Day twenty-five.

26.title: Dust and breath (Genesis 2:4–7)
26.hook: the first human is shaped from adamah, the earth, and given breath
26.howItsDone: Jews read the second creation story in the first Torah portion each autumn; each morning's prayers begin by thanking God for returning the soul, the neshamah, and the Hasidic teaching of the two pockets is often retold.

segments.voice: Yesterday: menuchah, the rest that finished the world. The first thing called holy was a day, not a place.

A potter at a wheel, or a kid at the beach, hands wet, shaping something out of mud. It's close work: thumbs pressing, the maker bent right over the thing being made. In the first chapter of Genesis, God makes the world from far away, by speaking. In the second, the camera comes down close. The story starts again, and God shapes a person, as it were, by hand. Then leans in closer still.
screen: `A POTTER, HANDS IN THE CLAY.` → `THE STORY STARTS AGAIN, CLOSE UP.` → `DUST, THEN BREATH.`

segments.voice: In the Jewish Publication Society's 1917 translation: "Then the LORD God formed man of the dust of the ground, and breathed into his nostrils the breath of life; and man became a living soul." Listen to the Hebrew. The ground is adamah. The human made from it is adam. At first adam isn't only a name; it's a word: the earthling, the one from the earth. And formed is the verb for a potter's work. Then God breathes into the nostrils, face to face, the breath of life, nishmat chayim. Neshamah, breath, is the same word Jews use for the soul. So the soul, in this picture, is a breath that came from very close. The Talmud adds that the dust for the first human was gathered from the whole earth. Rashi gives a reason: so that wherever a person dies, the ground will take them in. Every land can be home. A Hasidic teacher, Rabbi Simcha Bunim of Peshischa, told his students to carry two slips of paper, one in each pocket. On one: for my sake the world was created, from the Mishnah on day twenty-four. On the other: I am but dust and ashes, Abraham's words to God on day eight. When you feel too proud, reach for the dust. When you feel worthless, reach for the other pocket. The trick is knowing which one. Earth and breath: in this teaching, both are true of a person, all the time.
screen: `ADAMAH — THE GROUND. ADAM — THE EARTHLING.` · `NESHAMAH — BREATH, AND SOUL.` · `DUST FROM THE WHOLE EARTH.` · `TWO POCKETS.` · then, large: `AND MAN BECAME A LIVING SOUL.`

segments.voice: Put both feet flat on the floor and feel them press toward the ground you're made of. Then breathe in slowly through your nose, and notice the air coming in close, the way the story says the first breath did. Feet, earth; nose, breath: stay with both.
Adam. The earthling, shaped from adamah, the ground, and given breath from very close.
Your line: earth and breath. Dust and a living soul, in one person. Until tomorrow.

27.title: Not good to be alone (Genesis 2:18–25)
27.hook: the first thing the Torah calls "not good" is loneliness
27.howItsDone: Jewish tradition treats companionship as a basic need: study is often done in pairs, called chavruta, many prayers are said in community, and visiting the sick is counted a mitzvah.

segments.voice: Yesterday: adam, the earthling, shaped from dust and given breath. Your line was earth and breath: dust and ashes in one pocket, the world created for my sake in the other.

So far, everything in this story has been good. Light, good. Land, good. Sun and moon, fish and birds, good. At the end of the sixth day, very good: seven times, as you heard on day six. Then the human is alone in the garden. Plenty to eat, nothing dangerous, nothing wrong, you'd think. And for the first time in the Torah, God looks at something and says it's not good. Not a sin. Not a monster. Not a flood.
screen: `GOOD, GOOD, VERY GOOD.` → `A HUMAN, ALONE IN A GARDEN.` → `THE FIRST NOT GOOD.`

segments.voice: In the Jewish Publication Society's 1917 translation: "It is not good that the man should be alone; I will make him a help meet for him." The first not good is loneliness. That old phrase, help meet, is often heard as a helper, an assistant. The Hebrew is ezer kenegdo. Ezer means help, and the Bible also uses it for God: "My help cometh from the LORD," say the Psalms, in the same translation. It's not a junior word. Kenegdo means opposite him, facing him; readers hear an equal in it, someone who can look you in the eye. Rashi noticed it can also mean against him, and gave a wry answer: if you're worthy, a help; if not, someone who pushes back. Then the animals come. The human names each one, and none of them is the one. The human sleeps, and a second person is made from the first, from the side, the text says. And the first human speaks the Torah's first human words, almost a song: "This is now bone of my bones, and flesh of my flesh." The rabbis carried the idea far beyond marriage. The Talmud tells of Honi, who slept for seventy years, woke, and found that nobody knew him anymore. It closes his story with a saying people used: either companionship, or death. Friends, study partners, community, family. People need people, and the Torah says so at the start, before anything else goes wrong.
screen: `THE FIRST NOT GOOD: ALONE.` · `EZER — THE WORD USED FOR GOD.` · `KENEGDO — FACING, AS AN EQUAL.` · `BONE OF MY BONES.` · then, large: `EITHER COMPANIONSHIP, OR DEATH.`

segments.voice: Who might be lonely right now? An older neighbor, a friend who moved away, a coworker who eats lunch alone, someone who went quiet in the group chat. Hold one of their faces in mind, and stay with them for a few slow breaths.
Ezer kenegdo: help that faces you as an equal. The first not good in the Torah, and the help that meets it.
Your line: not good alone. People need people, from the very first pages. See you on day twenty-eight.

screen: `DAY 27 COUNTS.` → `TOMORROW: THE GARDEN AND THE QUESTION.`

28.title: The garden and the question (Genesis 3)
28.hook: the fruit, the hiding, and God's first question to a person: "Where art thou?"
28.howItsDone: Jews read the garden story in the first Torah portion each autumn; the question ayekah, where are you, is a theme of sermons and Hasidic teaching as a call to honest self-examination.

segments.voice: Yesterday: ezer kenegdo, help that faces you as an equal. The first not good was being alone.

It's quiet. Too quiet. A parent finds a small child behind the couch, very still, chocolate on their face. The parent knows what happened. The child knows the parent knows. And still the parent asks: where are you? In the garden, the two humans were told not to eat from one tree. A snake starts a conversation. They eat. Their eyes are opened, they see they're naked, and they sew fig leaves together. Then, in the cool of the day, they hear God walking in the garden, and they hide.
screen: `TOO QUIET.` → `THE FRUIT, THE FIG LEAVES.` → `THEY HIDE AMONG THE TREES.`

segments.voice: First, a myth to clear up: the text never says apple. Just fruit. The rabbis guessed a fig, since fig leaves were right there, or grapes, or wheat, or a citron. The apple is a later picture, not the text's. Now the moment everything turns on. In the Jewish Publication Society's 1917 translation: "And the LORD God called unto the man, and said unto him: 'Where art thou?'" In Hebrew, one word: ayekah. It's the first question God asks a human being in the Torah, and it's strange, because God obviously knows where he is. One answer in Jewish teaching: the question isn't for God. It's for the man, a door left ajar: come out and say where you are. And what does he do with the door? He answers, then points: the woman you gave me, she gave me the fruit. The woman points at the snake. The first question, and the first blame, passed along like a hot plate. There's a Hasidic story. The founder of Chabad, Rabbi Shneur Zalman of Liadi, was in a Russian prison, and an official questioning him asked why God, who knows everything, would ask Adam where he was. The rabbi answered: in every age, God calls to every person: where are you in your world? So many years of your life have passed. Where are you? This week: Bereshit, yom, tzelem Elohim, menuchah, adam, ezer kenegdo, and now the first question, still hanging in the air.
screen: `NOT AN APPLE. JUST FRUIT.` · `AYEKAH — WHERE ARE YOU?` · `THE QUESTION IS A DOOR.` · `THE FIRST BLAME, PASSED ALONG.` · then, large: `WHERE ART THOU?`

segments.voice: Let the question land, not as an accusation but as a door left open: where are you in your life right now? Is there anything you're hiding behind, and what would it take to step out from behind the tree? You don't have to answer out loud, only honestly.
Ayekah: Hebrew for where are you, the first question God asks a person. The fruit, the hiding, and a door left open.
Your line: where are you. That's day twenty-eight, and with it, week four is done.

God asks because God doesn't know where Adam is
one Jewish reading: the question is for the man, a door left open.

fork.setup: you're Adam. God has just asked, "where art thou?" what does the man actually do?
options: confesses right away and says sorry.
answers, and then blames the woman.
stays silent behind the tree.
fork.reveal: he answers, then points: the woman you gave me. she points at the snake. the first blame, passed along.

original.note: Hebrew: where are you? one word, the first question God asks a person.

trapdoor: what you thought: the story of the apple.
what it means: two people hide, and God asks a question God already knows the answer to, so they can come out.
what a scholar hears: the fruit is unnamed; Berakhot 40a and Genesis Rabbah 15:7 guess fig, grape, wheat, citron. Hasidic tradition reads ayekah as a call to every person in every age.
guess: where art thou, God's first question
why did you eat, God's first rebuke
a cry of shame from the one hiding

sources.ref: Babylonian Talmud, Berakhot 40a; Genesis Rabbah 15:7 (what the fruit was)
